questions.question:
The speaker told a joke to break the ice at the start of the meeting.

The idiom "break the ice" in this sentence means
options: ease the tension and begin the conversation
questions.explanation: A joke at the start eases the awkwardness so that people can talk.

questions.question:
Passing the quiz was a piece of cake for her.

The idiom "a piece of cake" in this sentence means
questions.explanation: The idiom means something that is extremely easy to do.

questions.question:
We go to that restaurant once in a blue moon.

The idiom "once in a blue moon" in this sentence means
questions.explanation: It means very rarely, not literally on the occasion of a blue moon.

questions.question:
Please don't spill the beans about the surprise party.

The idiom "spill the beans" in this sentence means
questions.explanation: To spill the beans is to reveal a secret.

questions.question:
I am feeling a bit under the weather today.

The idiom "under the weather" in this sentence means
questions.explanation: It means feeling slightly ill.

questions.question:
You hit the nail on the head when you said the problem was poor planning.

The idiom "hit the nail on the head" in this sentence means
questions.explanation: It means to be exactly right about something.

questions.question:
She has been burning the midnight oil to finish her thesis.

The idiom "burning the midnight oil" in this sentence means
questions.explanation: It means working late at night.

questions.question:
He decided to bite the bullet and tell his manager about the mistake.

The idiom "bite the bullet" in this sentence means
questions.explanation: It means to do something difficult or unpleasant that cannot be avoided.

questions.question:
The designer jewellery cost an arm and a leg.

The idiom "cost an arm and a leg" in this sentence means
questions.explanation: It means to cost a very large amount.

questions.question:
I have sent you the offer; now the ball is in your court.

The idiom "the ball is in your court" in this sentence means
options: it is your turn to act or decide
questions.explanation: It means the next move belongs to you.

questions.question:
The builder was accused of cutting corners on the project.

The idiom "cutting corners" in this sentence means
options: doing something cheaply or carelessly to save time or money
questions.explanation: It means skipping steps or standards to save effort or cost.

questions.question:
Stop beating around the bush and tell me what happened.

The idiom "beating around the bush" in this sentence means
questions.explanation: The speaker wants a direct answer, so the idiom means avoiding the point.

questions.question:
On the question of moving to a new city, she is still on the fence.

The idiom "on the fence" in this sentence means
questions.explanation: It means not having made up one's mind.

questions.question:
The workers decided to call it a day when the rain started.

The idiom "call it a day" in this sentence means
questions.explanation: It means to stop working for the day.

questions.question:
After three failed attempts, he threw in the towel.

The idiom "threw in the towel" in this sentence means
questions.explanation: To throw in the towel is to give up.

questions.question:
Nobody mentioned the budget crisis, though it was the elephant in the room.

The idiom "the elephant in the room" in this sentence means
options: an obvious problem that no one wants to discuss
questions.explanation: It refers to a major issue that everyone knows about but avoids.

questions.question:
Losing that job turned out to be a blessing in disguise.

The idiom "a blessing in disguise" in this sentence means
options: something that seems bad but turns out good
questions.explanation: It describes a misfortune that brings an unexpected benefit.

questions.question:
By quarrelling with every client, he burned his bridges in the industry.

The idiom "burned his bridges" in this sentence means
options: destroyed the chance of returning or getting help
questions.explanation: It means ruining relationships so that return is impossible.

questions.question:
I don't believe it, but let me play devil's advocate and argue the other side.

The idiom "play devil's advocate" in this sentence means
options: argue the opposite view for the sake of argument
questions.explanation: It means arguing against a view, often to test it, without necessarily believing the argument.

questions.question:
If you think I took your pen, you are barking up the wrong tree.

The idiom "barking up the wrong tree" in this sentence means
options: making a mistake in what you are pursuing
questions.explanation: It means choosing the wrong course or blaming the wrong person.
